newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wheat crop seen hit by El Nino effect.
newsitem.headline: Australian wheat crop seen hit by El Nino effect.

text.p: Forecasts of renewed drought in Australia because of warming sea temperatures in the Pacific are forcing a dramatic reappraisal of the size of Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop from officially-predicted near-record levels.

Barely a week after the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) forecast a bumper crop of 19.2 million tonnes, fears are emerging that the so-called El Nino effect could reduce the crop to 14 million tonnes or even less.
Only hours after ABARE released its crop forecast on June 3, the Bureau of Meteorology reported that Australia was in the grip of a persistent and strengthening El Nino weather event.

ABARE officials told Reuters on Wednesday the forecast 19.2 million tonne wheat crop for 1997/98, not far behind the record 23.5 million tonne crop which Australia brought in in 1996/97, did not take into account the prospect of an El Nino drought.
The ABARE forecast was based on asumptions of normal seasonal conditions and normal yields, officials said.

They noted that a table in the June 3 report outlined five possible weather outcomes, ranging from very dry El Nino to average. The official 19.2 million tonne forecast was based on the fifth possible outcome, of average weather, they said.
An El Nino weather pattern - considered less likely - would produce a crop of 16.3 million tonnes, ABARE figures showed.
The Bureau of Meteorology said the El Nino pattern "will persist for the remainder of the year".
"A continuation of the El Nino would have serious consequences for Australia," the weather bureau said.

El Nino, or "boy child" in Spanish, relates to warm water which appears off the South American coast near Peru and Ecuador, and reacts with atmospheric temperatures. This causes changed air circulations across the Pacific Ocean, Indonesia and eastern Australia and is associated with drought.

ABARE's 16.3 million tonne forecast, as a dry weather possibility, was not based on the prospect of a bad drought but on a median of historical periods where dry conditions had occurred, an ABARE official said.
Actual rainfall could be better than that or worse than that, the official said.

Reflecting growing market and trade concern, Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said on Wednesday that if Australia experienced protracted El Nino drought, the 1997/98 wheat crop could emerge at 14.5 million tonnes at best.
"Reality is that 14.5 million tonnes is an optimistic point of view (if an El Nino-produced drought occurs)," he said.
An official with a state grains marketing body, who asked not to be identified, also discounted the ABARE forecast.
"It doesn't matter what (crop) is, it's going to be all decimated if El Nino comes in," the official said.
"I think (ABARE's forecasts are) all very optimistic. If it rains, then they're well within their bounds," he said.
"But if the drought comes, the predictions will be a long way off, I'd suggest three to four million tonnes (off for) wheat," he added.
Drought-affected Australian wheat yields plummet to about 1.47 tonnes a hectare from about 1.74 tonnes in average years.
ABARE forecasts Australian farmers will sow 11.1 million hectares to wheat in 1997/98, down slightly from the 11.3 million hectares last year.
Opinions in the grains industry are divided.
Private forecaster Brian Bailey of Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd said on Wednesday that he still agreed with the approximate range of ABARE's wheat forecast.
Bailey noted that weather predicting skills were still developing.
